sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on "Library opening hours" (top left, ~96,60), then goes down a single left column of three bold branch names, each with two plain lines under it. It reads as a plain public-information page from a local library. It feels calm and plain. The right two-thirds and the bottom ~280 px are empty. On reading the lines, the times are spelled out in words, and the Mobile library has no times at all.

Job (assumed): a resident checks quickly when a given branch is open.

The whole piece:
- One sentence purpose: yes
- Image and headline one idea: yes (no image, so the line is met)
- Every element does a job: yes
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished: **no**. Mobile library lines (96,458 and 96,503) give a day and a place but no hours. "nine to eight" / "ten to four" don't say am or pm, and spelled-out times are slow to scan. Days the branches are closed are never stated.
- Each kind of element looks the same everywhere: yes
- Mood fits the message: yes
- Headings name their sections: yes

The only `no` line names no catalog entry, so there are no entries to open. I'm judging it as common sense.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the copy finished, with no placeholder text and no spelling mistakes?** No. The hours are incomplete and can be read two ways. Where: the Mobile library block at x≈96, y≈413–515, and all six hour lines at y≈188–503.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The Mobile library lines ("Wednesday at the market square", "Thursday at the school gates") say where the van is but not when. Anyone who wants to catch it can't act on this page.
   - **Two readings:** The branch hours are written as words ("nine to eight", "ten to four", "ten to six", "ten to two") with no am or pm. Most people will guess right, but each line needs a moment of parsing instead of a glance.
   - **Unstated closed days:** The page never says which days are closed. Harbour branch is presumably closed Sunday and Monday, and Main branch on Sunday. Viewers have to work that out from what's missing, and someone checking "is Harbour open Monday?" has to deduce a no.
   - **Why it matters:** This is a page whose whole job is times. Times are what people act on and hold the library to, so ambiguity here is a defect, not a style note. This is common sense; no catalog entry covers it.
   - **Fix:** Give the mobile stops their hours. Write times as numerals with am/pm, or 24-hour (e.g. "9 am – 8 pm"), so they scan in a glance. State the closed days outright ("Closed Sunday and Monday").
   - Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- **One clear purpose:** One heading and three named groups make the page self-evident. Nobody has to wonder what it is or which branch a line belongs to.
- **Nothing extra:** No ornament, boxes or dividers. Weight and spacing alone set the bold branch names apart from their lines, so every element earns its place.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the page is part of a larger site. The large empty area to the right and below the list could be fine inside a site frame, or could be an unfinished layout.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (copy finished: mobile library has no hours, times have no am/pm, closed days aren't stated)

**Walk (working notes).** I read the image whole. Bash was refused, so I skipped the crop script. The image is about one screen (about 1280×800), so the whole image is enough.

First read: the eye lands on "Library opening hours", which is bold and about 28 px, at the top left. It then drops into a single left-aligned column of evenly spaced lines. The bold branch names stand out as you scan down. It reads as a plain, calm information page. My assumption about its job: a library web page where a visitor can find when and where each branch is open.

- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? **Yes.** The title is the only large size and clearly dominates.
- Can you tell each level of the text from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same? **Yes.** There are two sizes with a big step between them: the title at about 28 px, and everything else at about 17 px. Headings and body share a size, but bold against regular separates them at a glance. No two sizes are close.
- Where headings are larger than the text, do they also differ in weight, form, or colour? **Yes.** The title is both larger and bold. The branch headings are not larger, so this only applies to the title.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly leads.** It is the only large size on the page, at about 28 px bold against about 17 px for everything else. That big step means the eye knows where to start and nothing competes with it (Bringhurst on a scale with real steps between sizes).
- **Headings are set apart by weight, not by another size.** "Main branch", "Harbour branch" and "Mobile library" are the same size as the hours but bold. That gives a third level without adding a size that would sit too close to the body (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger). Keep this when revising rather than enlarging the headings slightly.

Note for the director, outside this section: every line, heading or not, sits on the same vertical spacing of about 45 px. So each branch heading is no closer to its own hours than to the line above it, and the three groups don't form. That belongs to Arrangement (grouping and spacing), not here.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. This is a single-column text page with one heading and three groups, each a subheading and two lines.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No. From "Main branch" (y≈143) to "Thursday at the school gates" (y≈503), every line sits about 45 px below the one before it. The gap between "Saturday, ten to four" and "Harbour branch" is the same as the gap between "Harbour branch" and "Tuesday to Friday…", and the same again between the two Mobile library lines. The nine lines read as one evenly spaced list, not three branches. Only the bold weight shows where a new group starts, and each subheading floats halfway between the group above and its own lines instead of sitting with them. A reader scanning for "when is Harbour open on Saturday?" has to read the labels to find the boundaries, because the space doesn't show them. With equal gaps everywhere, the groups disappear (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II "Shape", proximity after Wertheimer). Fix: make the gap within a group clearly smaller than the gap between groups. Pull each branch's two lines tight to their subheading, at about normal line spacing, and add a clearly larger space, roughly double, above "Harbour branch" and "Mobile library". The title-to-first-group gap (≈65 px, y≈77→143) can stay as it is or grow a little. Defect. Weight: major. This spacing is the only arrangement decision on the page, and it is what makes three schedules read as three schedules.

**What's working.** Everything hangs from one clean left edge at x≈96: title, subheadings and items, with no near-misses. The column reads top to bottom with nothing pulling the eye elsewhere. That single flush-left axis suits a short reference list and should stay.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The content fills only the top-left third of a 1280×800 frame, leaving the right two-thirds and the bottom empty. On a left-aligned web page that reads normally rather than lopsided, so I didn't count it as a balance problem. Still, check whether this frame is the intended context (a page, a sign, a kiosk screen). If it's a standalone display, the empty field would need deciding on purpose.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups)

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**

All 30 Text checklist lines pass. The problems below are in the copy, which the checklist doesn't cover. They're included because opening hours are exactly what a visitor will act on.

1. **Opening times are written as words, and there's no morning or afternoon.** This affects all four time lines: "Monday to Friday, nine to eight" (y≈188), "Saturday, ten to four" (y≈233), "Tuesday to Friday, ten to six" (y≈323) and "Saturday, ten to two" (y≈368). Someone checking hours scans for numbers, and "nine to eight" makes them read the whole sentence instead. It also never says morning or afternoon. "Ten to two" can be read as a time of day (1:50), not a range, and "ten to six" has the same problem. Read the wrong way, someone turns up at the wrong time or thinks the branch is shut. This is a **defect** (common sense, plus the critic brief's rule that times and dates must not be readable two ways). Fix: use figures with a clear range, such as "9 am – 8 pm" or "09:00–20:00", with a real en dash. Pick one format and use it for every line. **Major.**
2. **The mobile library lines give a place and day but no time.** "Wednesday at the market square" and "Thursday at the school gates" (y≈458–503) don't say when the van is there. "School gates" suggests a short window around school hours, so a visitor can't plan to catch it. **Defect** (common sense). Fix: add the hours to each line, e.g. "Wednesday, 10 am – 1 pm, market square". **Major.**
3. **The days a branch is closed are left for the reader to work out.** Main branch lists Monday to Saturday, and Harbour lists Tuesday to Saturday. Sunday at both, and Monday at Harbour, are only implied. A visitor who doesn't notice that Harbour starts on Tuesday may make a wasted trip on a Monday. **Defect**, weak (common sense). Fix: add a line such as "Closed Sunday and Monday" to Harbour, and "Closed Sunday" to Main. **Minor.**

**What's working.**
- Everything is in one sans-serif family. Branch names are marked by weight only (bold at roughly the body size), not by a new size or face, so the type stays calm and has only three levels: title, branch name, line. This is the "bolder, not bigger" approach from Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*.
- The body text is about 18 px, near-black on white, and set flush left. It's easy to read at a glance, with no contrast or size problems.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

The eye lands first on "Library opening hours" at the top left. It then runs down the column of bold branch names. The piece reads as a plain web page or notice listing the hours of a local library, with near-black text on white and no hue anywhere. My assumption is that it tells library users when and where each branch is open.

**Walk: Color** (whole image, 1280 × 800, no crops needed)
- Small palette: yes. It uses one neutral, near-black on white, and no hue.
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes. There is no saturated color.
- Clear range of light and dark, structure shows in grayscale: yes. Dark text on white gives full contrast, and the structure comes from weight, so it survives grayscale as it is.
- Warm forward, cool recedes: yes. There are no temperatures in play.
- Matching colors look the same everywhere: yes. Headings and body text appear to share one near-black, judged by eye.
- Neighboring strong colors differ in lightness: yes. There are no strong colors next to each other.
- Status colors used only for their meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. Branch names are marked by bold weight, not color.
- Dark theme uses dark gray, not pure black: yes. This is a light theme, so the line does not apply.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so I opened no entries.

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is entirely neutral: near-black type on a white ground.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Contrast:** the single near-black on white gives the highest practical contrast for the body lines at about 18 px (x 96–376, y 180–515). Every time and place stays easy to read, and nothing competes with the information.
- **Weight carries the grouping, not color:** the branch labels "Main branch", "Harbour branch" and "Mobile library" at y ≈ 143, 278 and 413 are set off by bold weight in the same color. The grouping still shows in grayscale and to colour-blind readers, which is "bolder, not bigger" in the sense Wathan and Schoger give it in *Refactoring UI*.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks. It is a text-only list of library opening hours: a heading, three bold branch names and six lines of hours on a white background.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
